lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Types of Waste and the Science of Managing Them

pages.body:
Walk around your school compound or your street and look at the rubbish on the ground, in the gutters and near the bins. Notice the smells and the insects.

- What kinds of waste can you see, and where do you think each one came from?
- What problems can this waste cause for the people who live or learn nearby?

Every community produces waste. Waste that is managed well keeps people healthy and the environment clean, and waste that is ignored causes disease and pollution. In this lesson we classify waste, study the problems it causes and learn the science behind good methods of managing it.

We begin with a meaning of waste and its main sources.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: What waste is and where it comes from

pages.title: What waste is and where it comes from
pages.body:
Waste is any material that is no longer wanted or useful and is thrown away. It comes from homes, schools, markets, farms, hospitals, industries and mines.

Next we group waste in three ways, by state, by how easily it breaks down and by how dangerous it is.

pages.title: Types of waste
pages.body:
- By state. Solid waste includes food remains, paper, plastic sachets, bottles, cans and scrap metal. Liquid waste includes bath and kitchen water, sewage, used oil and factory effluent. Gaseous waste includes smoke and fumes from vehicles, factories and burning rubbish.
- By breakdown. Biodegradable waste can be broken down by living things such as bacteria and fungi. It includes food remains, leaves and animal droppings. Nonbiodegradable waste cannot easily be broken down. It includes plastics, glass, metals and rubber.
- By danger. Hazardous waste is harmful to people or the environment. It includes batteries, chemicals, pesticide containers, used oil, hospital waste and old electronic equipment.

We then see why waste management is a science and public health issue.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Problems caused by poor waste management

pages.title: Problems caused by poor waste management
pages.body:
- Blocked gutters and drains cause floods during heavy rain.
- Rubbish heaps and stagnant water collect houseflies, mosquitoes and rats that spread diseases such as cholera, typhoid, diarrhoea and malaria.
- Waste thrown into rivers, lagoons and the sea pollutes the water and harms fish.
- Plastic waste harms animals that swallow it and stays in the soil for a very long time.
- Open burning of rubbish releases smoke and poisonous gases that cause breathing problems.
- Chemicals and used oil can pollute the soil and underground water.

Finally we study methods of managing each type of waste and the science that explains why they work.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Managing waste and the science behind each method

pages.title: Managing waste and the science behind each method
pages.body:
| **Method** | **How it works** | **Science behind it** |
|---|---|---|
| Reduce, reuse and recycle | Use less, use things again and turn used materials into new products. Plastics, glass, metals and paper can be collected, melted or pulped and remade | Melting is a physical change. Recycling saves raw materials and the energy needed to make new products |
| Sorting at source | Separate food waste, recyclable materials and general waste into different bins | Different materials need different treatment, and mixing them makes treatment harder |
| Composting | Heap leaves and food waste in layers, keep them moist and turn them to let in air. After some weeks a dark crumbly compost forms that is used as manure | Bacteria and fungi decompose organic matter using oxygen, which releases nutrients and some heat |
| Biogas production | Animal dung and food waste are placed in a closed tank where gas collects and can be used for cooking | Bacteria break down waste without oxygen and produce methane, a fuel gas |
| Sanitary landfill | Waste is placed in a prepared pit with a lining, compacted and covered with soil each day | The lining stops harmful liquids from entering the ground. Covering reduces smell and stops pests |
| Incineration | Waste, especially hospital waste, is burned at very high temperature in a closed furnace with filters | High temperature destroys germs and reduces volume. Filters trap harmful gases |
| Sewage treatment and septic tanks | Solid matter settles or is screened out, and bacteria break down the rest. The water is disinfected before it is released | Settling separates solids from liquid. Bacteria digest the organic matter and disinfectant kills germs |
| Treating gaseous waste | Use filters in chimneys, service vehicles, use cleaner fuels and plant trees | Filters trap particles. Trees take in carbon dioxide during photosynthesis |
| Hazardous waste | Take batteries, used oil and old electronic devices to proper collection points | These contain poisonous substances such as lead and mercury, which must not enter soil or water |

lessons.title: Types of Waste and the Science of Managing Them (part 5)

> **Did you know?** Burning electronic waste such as cables to get the metal inside releases toxic smoke. This is a serious health problem at some e waste sites, for example in parts of Accra, and is why old electronics should be taken to proper recycling points.

pages.body:
A school finds that the compound is littered with sachet water bags and food wrappers, and the drains are choked. The head teacher asks learners to find a long lasting solution.

- What steps would you take to find out how much waste is produced and where it comes from?
- How would you know that your project has worked?

Knowing about waste is not enough. We must use what we know to make our school and community cleaner. In this lesson we plan and carry out a waste management project and then write a report on what we achieved.

We start by finding out what works elsewhere.

pages.title: Researching good practices
pages.body:
- Use the library, the internet and local experts such as the school health coordinator or officers of the district assembly.
- Find out how other schools and towns sort, reuse, compost and recycle waste.
- Write down the practices that suit your school and the materials they need.

Now we plan the project in clear stages.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Planning and carrying out a project

pages.title: Planning and carrying out a project
pages.body:
1. Decide on the aim, for example, to reduce the amount of rubbish thrown on the compound and to start a compost heap.
2. Carry out a survey for one week. Record the types and approximate amounts of waste collected each day.
3. Place labelled bins for food waste, recyclable materials and general waste in suitable places.
4. Build a compost heap with leaves and food waste in alternating layers, keep it moist like a squeezed sponge and turn it every one or two weeks.
5. Collect clean plastic bottles and cans for recycling or for reuse, such as seedling pots or pencil holders.
6. Make posters and hold short talks to teach other learners the rules.
7. Repeat the survey after four weeks and compare it with the first one.

[[pic: Photo style illustration of learners carrying out a school clean up. Some sort waste into three labelled bins and others build a compost heap with a spade. Wear gloves and boots.]]

> **Safety** Wear gloves and closed shoes when handling waste. Never pick up broken glass, needles or hospital waste with bare hands, and do not burn rubbish. Wash your hands with soap after the work.

Finally we communicate our results in a short report that we can present.

pages.title: Writing the report
pages.body:
- Title. For example, A Report on the Waste Management Project at our School.
- Introduction. State the problem, the aim and the date of the project.
- Method. Explain the steps you followed and who took part.
- Results. Present the surveys as tables or bar charts. Show the amount of each type of waste before and after the project.
- Discussion. Explain the changes and the science behind the methods used, such as composting and sorting.
- Conclusion and recommendations. State what was achieved and what should be done next.

| **Type of waste** | **Before the project** | **After the project** | **Change** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Food waste |  |  |  |
| Plastic sachets and bottles |  |  |  |
| Paper |  |  |  |
| Other |  |  |  |

Present your report to the class or at a school assembly using your chart or poster as a visual aid. Be ready to answer questions about the science behind each method you used.

pages.body:
- Waste is any unwanted material that is thrown away. It comes from homes, schools, markets, farms, hospitals, industries and mines.
- Waste may be solid, liquid or gaseous. It may be biodegradable or nonbiodegradable, and some is hazardous.
- Poor waste management causes floods, diseases, water and soil pollution, air pollution and harm to animals.
- Methods of managing waste include reducing, reusing, recycling, sorting, composting, biogas production, sanitary landfill, incineration, sewage treatment and the safe collection of hazardous waste.
- Composting depends on bacteria and fungi that decompose waste with oxygen. Biogas comes from bacteria that work without oxygen.
- A good project begins with research and a survey, uses simple methods such as sorting and composting and ends with a written report.
